lines: The class video now rides with you: YouTube, locked to the ride clock.
At seven minutes, with a twelve-second offset, the video is at seven twelve. The clock leads; the video follows.
The player comes from YouTube's privacy-enhanced domain, with no controls, out of the tab order. The ride controls it.
Every tick, the drift is checked. More than one and a half seconds either way, and the video seeks back.
If YouTube is blocked, or the video fails, the cover stays, and a notice says so.
The bike still follows the class: the clock reaches seven minutes, and the recovery's level goes to the bike.
The player lives in its own video library, loaded only when a ride plays its video.
A first view query would have added a kilobyte to the first load, so the frame is found another way.
In the tests, a fake YouTube player runs on the page's clock, so no request leaves the machine.
On a phone the video sits above the panel. From laptop width, it fills the column.
What the tests prove: four new specs and a table of drift cases, and every check is green.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
